speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Howzit, everybody, and welcome back to seven-eight-seven Flight Deck Notes. I'm Pualani — that's poo-ah-LAH-nee — coming to you from Honolulu, where the trades are blowing and the Kona's already poured. Today we go talk story about eff oh em Chapter 2, Operating-General. Da kine chapter that decides who's actually in charge of your airplane. And on our seven-eight-seven — the combined Alaska and Hawaiian jet, Hawaiian-operated, flying HNL out over the whole Pacific — that question really matters. Because by the time you augment across the water, "in charge" can literally change seats mid-ocean.

speaker: Chester
text: [warm] And I'm Chester, coming to you from a rainy Seattle window with a fresh pour-over. Or — hang on — Pualani mailed me a bag of Kona beans last week, so today it's a Kona pour. Don't tell my barista. Chapter 2 is one of the big high-yield ones, so grab your coffee. This is where the eff oh em lays out operational control, pee eye see authority, the chain of command, and the Operational Control Window. All of it.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] I'm Otto. And before anyone asks — yes, same name as the autopilot in Airplane! No, I do not inflate. And no, I have not got the aircraft. Yet. Surely we can start now.

speaker: Chester
text: [laughs] Don't call him Shirley.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] I told you never to call me Shirley. Right on cue, Chester.

speaker: Pualani
text: [laughs] Shoots. Okay Otto, you're our skeptic today, so keep us honest. Chester, kick us off. What even IS operational control?

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Straight from eff oh em 2.1: operational control, with respect to a flight, means the exercise of authority over initiating, conducting, or terminating a flight. Those three verbs are the whole ballgame. Initiating, conducting, terminating.

speaker: Pualani
text: [excited] And that's memory aid number one, everybody, so write 'em down. I-C-T. Initiating, Conducting, Terminating. I tell my students think of it like a canoe trip — you gotta launch it, paddle it, and beach it. ICT. Same three verbs every time it shows up — and it shows up again in eff oh em 2.2.1, word for word.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] So who actually holds that authority? Because "the exercise of authority" is lovely, but somebody's name has to be on it.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Good — eff oh em 2.1 again. The 14 see eff are Part 119 designated Director of Operations, the DO, has the authority for the supervision and control of all Alaska Airlines flights. All of them. And the DO has delegated the authority to conduct certain functions to the Flight Operations Duty Officer — the FODO.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Chur. DO at the top, delegates down to the FODO. So the DO's just handed the airplane to the FODO. Which means, for the record, I've got the aircraft. Figuratively.

speaker: Pualani
text: [laughs] Otto, you don't got nothing.

speaker: Otto
text: [deadpan] I've got it figuratively. It's a whole thing. You'll see.

speaker: Chester
text: [warm] And notice how the eff oh em keeps a name on it. eff oh em 2.2.1 says the FODO serves as a direct representative of the Director of Operations. So when you're talking to the FODO, you're basically talking with the DO's authority. Nobody's got it "figuratively." Somebody's always got it for real.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Da chain runs deep. And that's the theme of the whole chapter — authority is never floating loose. It's always assigned to a human being with a title.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Which is precisely why my bit is funny. Anyway. Carry on.

speaker: Chester
text: [warm] Now here's the part every check airman loves — joint responsibility. eff oh em 2.1.1. The pee eye see and the Aircraft Dispatcher are jointly responsible for the preflight planning, delay, and Dispatch Release of a flight.

speaker: Otto
text: [skeptical] Hang on. Jointly. So it's not the captain's airplane and the dispatcher just books the fuel?

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Correct — it's genuinely shared. Per eff oh em 2.1.1 they're jointly responsible for determining the suitability of weather, field and traffic conditions, airway facilities, and the filed route. And the agreement that the flight can be accomplished safely is indicated by the signatures of the pee eye see and Dispatcher on the Dispatch Release. Two signatures, one release.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Like both paddlers gotta agree before the canoe leaves the beach.

speaker: Otto
text: [serious] Chester, tell me about a time you actually saw that joint responsibility get tested. Not the theory. A real disagreement.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Oh, I've got one. Redeye out of Seattle, Seattle to HNL, seven-eight-seven full of people who want to wake up in Hawaii. My dispatcher had a beautiful release — legal fuel, legal alternate, everything squared. But sitting in the flight deck I'm watching the Honolulu forecast trend the wrong way. Kona low sliding in, low ceilings and rain earlier than the taff said. On paper the flight could be accomplished safely. In my gut, the margins were getting thin over five and a half hours of ocean.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] And you just launched anyway, because Hawaii?

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Opposite. eff oh em 2.1.1 — when conditions change and the flight can't be conducted per the Dispatch Release, the person encountering or learning of the changed conditions must contact the other to institute the amendment. I saw it first, so I owned the call. I picked up the phone to my dispatcher.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] And the dispatcher just rolled over?

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Also opposite. He pushed back — his data still supported the release. And that's the whole point: neither of us can steamroll the other, because both the pee eye see and the Dispatcher must agree the flight as planned can be accomplished safely. We didn't agree yet. So we didn't sign yet. We reworked it — bumped the alternate to a field that was staying clear, added contingency fuel — and then both of us were comfortable. Two signatures. Off we went into the dark.

speaker: Pualani
text: [excited] I love that, because it shows the eff oh em working exactly the way it's drawn. And notice — when the pee eye see has an issue related to operational control, eff oh em 2.1.1 says the pee eye see should contact the Dispatcher. The Dispatcher is the primary source of information related to the status of a flight. Not crew scheduling. Not the gate agent. The Dispatcher.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] And if the weather turns to custard halfway across the Pacific, after you've already launched?

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Same rule, eff oh em 2.1.1 — whoever encounters or learns of the changed conditions contacts the other to institute the amendment. On a long over-water seven-eight-seven leg, that's often the relief pilot pulling fresh weather in cruise. You learn it, you own the call. No waiting around for the other guy.

speaker: Otto
text: [serious] There's a sharper one buried in 2.1.1 though. The pee eye see may not allow a flight to continue toward a dispatched airport if it can't be completed safely due to hazardous conditions. What's the exception?

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] The exception is right there in eff oh em 2.1.1: unless, in the opinion of the pee eye see, there is no safer procedure. And then — this is the line every oral hits — in that event, continuation toward that airport is an emergency.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Ho, let me tell you about a time that one came alive. Fictional, but the numbers all real. Captain friend of mine, HNL down to Papeete — PPT, Tahiti, deep South Pacific. And the thing about the South Pacific is the alternates are far apart. You got Bora Bora, you got Rarotonga, and then a whole lot of ocean. She's descending toward Tahiti and PPT drops below minimums, weather worse than forecast. Her filed alternate's now marginal, and the fuel to reach the next real field is right on the ragged edge.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] So she's out of good options.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] She's out of good options. She looks at every single one, and there just is no safer procedure than pressing to Tahiti and getting it on the ground. So she does what eff oh em 2.1.1 says — the moment "no safer procedure" is your honest reason, you say the word. She declared. Continuation became an emergency.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] So the second "no safer option" becomes your reason for pressing on, you're not continuing a flight anymore. You're flying an emergency.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] And here's where eff oh em 2.2.8.1 backs her up — in the pee eye see job description, the Captain may unilaterally exercise emergency authority. Unilaterally. No committee. No phone call for permission. She already had the authority the second she needed it.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] That's the eff oh em telling you: label it what it is, and use the authority you already carry. No sugarcoat, no hesitation.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Beautiful. And to be clear, during all of that, I did not have the aircraft. She did. Legally and figuratively.

speaker: Chester
text: [warm] Let's talk pee eye see authority proper. eff oh em 2.1.2. The pee eye see has full control and authority in the operation of the aircraft, without limitation, over other crewmembers and their duties during flight time — whether or not they hold valid certificates authorizing them to perform those duties.

speaker: Otto
text: [skeptical] Without limitation. That's a big phrase. Even over someone not certificated for the job?

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Even then. Crewmembers shall comply with the pee eye see's orders. It's the eff oh em's echo of 14 see eff are 91.3.

speaker: Pualani
text: [serious] But listen to the flip side, same section, eff oh em 2.1.2 — if the pee eye see is not sure that any aspect of flight operations can be safely executed and in compliance with regulations, then the operation will be stopped. Not "maybe." Not "let's see." Will be stopped.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] So all that authority exists mainly so the captain can say no. I like that. Your ego's not writing any checks there.

speaker: Pualani
text: [laughs] Top Gun in the flight deck, I see you Otto. Your ego's writing a check — the eff oh em's telling you don't cash it.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] "That's right, Ice… man. I am dangerous." Only I'm dangerous by refusing the takeoff. Far less cinematic. No fly-bys.

speaker: Chester
text: [warm] One curveball in eff oh em 2.1.2 — the note. Any time a training or evaluation event is being conducted by a Check Pilot from a pilot seat, the Check Pilot is the designated pee eye see. So on a check ride, the authority shifts to the Check Pilot in the seat.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Ah. So on IOE, the Check Pilot's got the aircraft. Which means I don't. Noted. Reluctantly.

speaker: Pualani
text: [excited] And that's your IOE tie-in, everybody. When you first fly the line on the seven-eight-seven — Operating Experience — there's a Check Pilot in the other seat. eff oh em 2.1.2 note means when they're running that event from a pilot seat, they are the designated pee eye see. So on IOE, know whose authority is whose that day.

speaker: Otto
text: [serious] Tell me about a time that mattered, Pualani. Because on paper it's trivia. In the seat?

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] In the seat it's everything. My IOE, honest — HNL to lax, my first real line legs on the seven-eight-seven. We're getting vectored into Los Angeles and Approach throws us a late runway change, off the two-fours over to the two-fives. Classic lax. And my brain just… locked. Froze for a second. Fresh on the airplane, task-saturated, deer in the headlights.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Which is the worst possible second to have two people wondering who's flying.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Exactly. But because my Check Pilot was the designated pee eye see per eff oh em 2.1.2, there was zero ambiguity. He just took it — "I have the aircraft" — reset the box for the new runway, made the call, clean. No two captains wrestling over the tiller at four hundred feet. That note exists so the flight deck never has a leadership gap during training. The authority already had a name on it before I ever froze.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] See, that's the chapter again. The airplane always belongs to somebody specific. Never to Otto.

speaker: Chester
text: [laughs] We're four minutes into your bit and it's already load-bearing.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Right — and how long does the pee eye see's authority actually last? Report to shutdown?

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] eff oh em 2.1.2.1, Duration of Command. The pee eye see's control and authority is in effect from the time they report for duty until the termination of the flight.

speaker: Pualani
text: [excited] Memory aid number two, everybody — "Report to Termination." R-to-T. It starts when you report for duty — not at pushback, not at the gate, the moment you report. And it runs all the way to termination of the flight. Report. To. Termination.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Reassuringly bookended. Sweet as.

speaker: Chester
text: [warm] Now the chain of command, eff oh em 2.1.3. The sequence goes: Captain, the pee eye see. Then the International Relief Officer, the eye are oh, slash Second in Command, the ess eye see. Then a pee eye see-qualified First Officer. Then the First Officer. Then the "A" Flight Attendant, the F-F-A. Then the rest of the Flight Attendants in descending order.

speaker: Otto
text: [skeptical] And on an augmented crew, when the captain goes to the bunk over the middle of the ocean — who's minding the store?

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] eff oh em 2.1.3 spells it out. On a flight with an augmented Flight Crew, when the assigned Captain begins their rest period, the eye are oh will become the acting Captain.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] So the eye are oh's not just a spare paddler. Captain goes to rest, eye are oh IS the captain for that stretch. On our seven-eight-seven — HNL to Sydney, to Auckland, to Tokyo Haneda, to Seoul — that's not exotic. That's a normal Tuesday over the water.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] So when the Captain's asleep, the eye are oh's got the aircraft. Genuinely, this time. Not figuratively. I want that on the record — there's a version of "somebody's got it" that's actually real, and it's never me.

speaker: Chester
text: [laughs] The self-awareness is growing.

speaker: Otto
text: [serious] Let me give you the story that makes it real. Fictional, numbers accurate. Augmented seven-eight-seven crew, Auckland up to Honolulu — AKL to HNL, roughly nine hours, so we're carrying an eye are oh. Home turf for me, by the way; I like leaving from Auckland, they spell things correctly there. Deep in cruise, middle of the Pacific, nearest decent diversion field a long way off. The assigned Captain is on a legit, scheduled rest break — and while he's back there, he has a genuine medical event. Chest, clammy, not good. He is not coming back to that seat. Now what?

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Now eff oh em 2.2.8.3 does the heavy lifting. The eye are oh is ess eye see of the aircraft, and if the Captain becomes incapacitated, the eye are oh will assume command, perform the Captain's duties, and assume the Captain's responsibilities. That's not a promotion ceremony. It's instant.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Which is exactly why the certificate matters. eff oh em 2.2.8.3 has a note — a Flight Crewmember holding a restricted ay tee pee certificate must not act as pee eye see or eye are oh.

speaker: Pualani
text: [excited] And that makes total sense, yeah? The eye are oh can end up acting Captain when the assigned Captain rests, and can flat-out assume command if the Captain becomes incapacitated. You no can have a restricted ay tee pee sitting in a seat that might inherit command over the Pacific. The rule's there before the emergency — so it's already true when the emergency comes.

speaker: Otto
text: [serious] That's the part that got me the first time I studied it. The eff oh em doesn't wait for the crisis to decide who's qualified. It's decided on the ground, at the gate, at report time. So mid-ocean, there's no debate. The eye are oh has the aircraft. Full stop.

speaker: Chester
text: [warm] Beautifully connected. Okay — the one everybody asks about on the oral. The Operational Control Window. OCW. eff oh em 2.2.2.1.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Go on then. When's the window open?

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] OCW starts two and a half hours — D-150 — prior to the scheduled departure time, and ends when the aircraft is blocked in at the destination airport.

speaker: Pualani
text: [excited] Okay here's my trick for D-150. The 150 is minutes. 150 minutes is two and a half hours. So D-150, then block-in at the gate — that's your window. Opens at 150 minutes before push, closes when you block in at destination.

speaker: Otto
text: [skeptical] And the exceptions? Because there's always a special case hiding in these.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] There is. eff oh em 2.2.2.1 — some flights need the Dispatch Release and ATS Flight Plan produced 180 minutes prior, and for those the OCW starts three hours. D-180. The list lives in 8.5.2.1.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] D-180. Three hours. So picture our HNL to Seoul — HNL to Incheon, Incheon. That's a South Korea flight, so the window opens at D-180, not D-150. Seoul gets the extra half hour of babysitting. And here's the Rev 125 change you need — the D-180 list is now South Korea departures, Amazon cargo, AND seven-eight-seven and A330 Europe departures. So this one IS us. Fly the airplane to Europe and you're on the three-hour window.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Standard is D-150, two and a half hours. D-180, three hours, for South Korea like HNL to Incheon, for Amazon cargo, and for our own Europe departures. Two numbers, and know which flights pull the bigger one.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] And why does the window matter? eff oh em 2.2.2.3. Within the OCW, any decision to cancel or modify the flight is an operational control action, which requires coordination and endorsement from the Dispatcher and the pee eye see. The FODO and Pilot Crew Scheduling provide guidance when required — and the Director of Operations is ultimately responsible.

speaker: Otto
text: [skeptical] So inside the window, the business side can't just cancel your flight on a whim?

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Right. Compare it to eff oh em 2.2.2.2 — before the OCW, canceling or modifying is a business decision initiated by the business operations work group of the NOC. It does not require coordination and endorsement from the operational control elements. But once you're inside that window, it flips. Now it needs the Dispatcher and the pee eye see.

speaker: Otto
text: [serious] Give the listeners the scenario, Chester, because this is a favorite check-airman trap.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Here it is, and let's set it on that Seoul flight so the numbers bite. HNL to Incheon — South Korea, so your window opened at D-180, three hours before push. Now you're sitting at D-90 — ninety minutes to departure. Are you inside the window? Yes. You've been inside it since D-180. The NOC business group decides your seven-eight-seven is worth more re-flowed somewhere else and wants to cancel it out from under you. Fair question on the oral: can they just do it?

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] And the answer is?

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] No. Inside the OCW, that cancel is an operational control action. Per eff oh em 2.2.2.3 it requires coordination and endorsement from the Dispatcher and the pee eye see, and the Director of Operations is ultimately responsible. Now move the clock. Same Seoul flight, but you're at D-200 — that's more than three hours out, so you're before the D-180 window. Now per eff oh em 2.2.2.2 it's a straight business decision and they can flow the airplane without your endorsement.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] That's the whole heart of it. Before the window, business drives. Inside the window, safety and operational control gotta sign off. Da line moves the moment you hit D-150 — or D-180 heading to Korea.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] And there's a lovely line that anchors all of it — eff oh em 2.2.1, the note at the end of the operational control section. Business objectives will not override safety concerns of the pee eye see, Dispatcher, or DO, who share legal responsibility for the flight.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] That's the spine of the whole chapter. And eff oh em 2.2.4 — the NOC and ess oh see see section — says it again in plain words: the safety and regulatory concerns of operational control always take precedence over administrative and business issues.

speaker: Pualani
text: [excited] Safety first, business second. Every time.

speaker: Otto
text: [serious] One more authority worth flagging — the FODO. eff oh em 2.2.8.5. The FODO is accountable to the Director of Operations for daily oversight of line flying operations, and — this is the teeth — has the authority to temporarily remove Flight Crews from flight operations.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] So the FODO no just gives advice. Can pull a crew right off the line. Real authority, delegated straight from the DO.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] So the FODO can take the aircraft away from you entirely. Which is more than I can do. Again — everyone in this chapter can hold the airplane except me.

speaker: Chester
text: [laughs] There it is. Let's land this with the hard thresholds — the numbers check airmen love. Sterile Flight Deck, eff oh em 2.3.12. Critical phases are ground operations involving pushback, towing, taxi, takeoff, and landing — plus all other flight operations conducted below 10,000 feet em ess el, except cruise flight.

speaker: Otto
text: [skeptical] Below ten thousand, sterile — except cruise. And the ground-hold gotcha?

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] The note in eff oh em 2.3.12 — the Flight Deck is not considered sterile during lengthy ground holds when the parking brake is set. So sitting on a ground stop at HNL with the brake parked, you can talk. Start rolling again below ten, you button it back up.

speaker: Pualani
text: [excited] And bank and pitch, eff oh em 2.3.14 — normal flying should not require bank angles greater than 30 degrees, or pitch attitude greater than 20 degrees nose up. Now, the aircraft may exceed 20 nose up under certain conditions or climb profiles — and a light seven-eight-seven off a short interisland-length leg out of Kona will absolutely rotate up past twenty and feel like a rocket — but normal handling? 30 and 20.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Thirty of bank, twenty nose up. No need for speed. No need to buzz the tower. Very sensible.

speaker: Pualani
text: [laughs] There's the Top Gun. Otto, you were a Maverick this whole time.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Negative, Pualani. I'm the fella in the tower saying "the pattern is full." Okay — recap time. Bring it home, Chester.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Operational control, eff oh em 2.1 — initiating, conducting, terminating. Memory aid number one: I-C-T. The DO has authority over all flights and delegates to the FODO, who per eff oh em 2.2.1 is the DO's direct representative. Joint responsibility, eff oh em 2.1.1 — pee eye see and Dispatcher, two signatures on the Dispatch Release, whoever learns of a change owns the amendment, and continuation into hazardous conditions with no safer procedure is an emergency.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] pee eye see authority, eff oh em 2.1.2 — full control without limitation, but if you're not sure it's safe or legal, the operation will be stopped. eff oh em 2.1.2 note — Check Pilot running a training event from a pilot seat is the designated pee eye see. And eff oh em 2.2.8.1 — the pee eye see may unilaterally exercise emergency authority. Duration of command, eff oh em 2.1.2.1 — memory aid number two, "Report to Termination." From when you report for duty until the flight terminates.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Chain of command, eff oh em 2.1.3 — Captain, eye are oh slash ess eye see, pee eye see-qualified eff oh, eff oh, A Flight Attendant, then the rest. Captain rests, the eye are oh becomes acting Captain. Captain incapacitated, eff oh em 2.2.8.3 — the eye are oh assumes command. And no restricted ay tee pee in the pee eye see or eye are oh seat.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] OCW, eff oh em 2.2.2.1 — D-150, two and a half hours before departure, closes at block-in. D-180, three hours, for South Korea, Amazon cargo, and seven-eight-seven Europe departures per 8.5.2.1. Inside the window, cancel or modify needs the Dispatcher and pee eye see per eff oh em 2.2.2.3, and the DO is ultimately responsible. Before the window, eff oh em 2.2.2.2, it's a business decision. And the FODO, eff oh em 2.2.8.5, can temporarily remove a crew.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Hard numbers — sterile flight deck below 10,000 except cruise, eff oh em 2.3.12. Bank 30, pitch 20 nose up, eff oh em 2.3.14. And safety always beats business — eff oh em 2.2.1 note and eff oh em 2.2.4. That's Chapter 2 in a nutshell.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Well. That was heaps more useful than I expected from a chapter titled "General."

speaker: Chester
text: [warm] And I'll admit it — this Kona Pualani sent me is better than my pour-over. Don't tell Seattle. I may have to fly to HNL just to restock.

speaker: Pualani
text: [laughs] Come for the beans, stay for the trades. Shoots! That's eff oh em Chapter 2, Operating-General. Study 'em, know your numbers, and we go see you next episode. Malama pono, everybody.

speaker: Chester
text: [warm] Fly safe out there.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] And remember — the airplane always belongs to somebody. A real, named, qualified human being. Never to me. I've got it… figuratively. Which, as we have now thoroughly established, means I've got nothing at all.
